chapter: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
title: Eddie Barefield punches him in the back at the Apollo
summary: At Christmas 1946, backstage at the Apollo, a drunken Barefield punches Cobb in the back; Cobb says he only told him last week and blames it for his later operation.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Yeah, well, now, you've said that your back was troubling you. Is this still the back from when you were hit by the -- all this time it was --
Well, I got another blow in New York to really captivate that thing in '46 Christmas. Eddie Barfield, and I didn't tell him until I was in New York (inaudible) --

was working at NBC as a man that go on all the shows and if he had to transpose to play this instrument, then he would -- he's a utility man you'd (inaudible) and he was off during the Christmas holidays. And I had been at the Braddock Bar, and I knew that 15 minutes was going in, so I left ten minutes prior because I said (inaudible) already.

And I'm going backstage to the Apollo Theater in the snow during the Christmas holidays, and he tipped up behind me and hit me on my back with his fist. I was gasping for wind. I'm telling you, I couldn't breathe. And this time I opened the number, Airmail Special, if you remember this. I'm gasping for breath, and I couldn't hardly play the first tune. It took me a long time to get (out inaudible), and I never told him nothing about it until just this last week.

He said, "I don't remember nothing." I said, "You were drunk." I said, "I didn't want to tell you. Now, I've had you -- we've been to Washington, D. C., to supplement my band, and augment it, the (inaudible), and I never told you nothing about it because wasn't nothing you could do about it after it happened, but I don't allow nobody to talk to me with their hands anymore, because that was a lot of damage was done to me."
He hit me, man, with his fists.
But it was a joke, though.
And I can't hear him coming behind me in the snow. He's tipping behind me in the snow and hit me and catch me by surprise, and I couldn't breathe on that first number, playing.
: Yeah, but he, of course, he's --
And that cost me a lot of money, playing, and cost me something to my health too.

He was a bull. Him and Ben Webster and Ben Carter wasn't nothing but football players. Them are the strongest saxophone players I know to sit up and manhandle the horn and wasn't on the field hitting somebody block and tackle. They were brutes, that's what they were. And now, he's drunk and playing with me.

And I told him. And he felt so bad. I said, I don't want you to feel bad. I've lived through it many a year now. But now I think I can tell you. You are responsible for me having that operation because you knocked the hell out of me, playing. That's the whole thing. But don't you know I held it all these years? I told him last week (inaudible). Wasn't that beautiful? What could he have done if I had told him? Nothing. He couldn't correct it. He couldn't do nothing that the doctor couldn't do. And the doctor was the one I had to go to and have the operation.
